objective: By the end you can explain what is agreed before the first brick (drawings, BOQ, rates, contract: advance, retention, defects period, delay) and why the BOQ is the yardstick for everything after.

scenes.title: The job is won
beats: Thrissur, the twentieth of October. Doctor Anand Krishnan signs a contract for his family's new house: Green Villa.
Eighty-two lakh rupees. Nine months. A two-storey villa, and a small annex beside it.
Not one brick is laid yet. But the things that decide whether this job makes money are already on paper. This episode is about that paper.

scenes.title: From drawings to a signed contract
beats: Every job starts as drawings. The architect draws what to build. The structural consultant sizes the footings, the columns and the steel.
From the drawings, the builder measures everything: so many cubic metres of excavation, so many square metres of plastering. That list is the bill of quantities: the BOQ.
Each line gets two prices. What the client will pay for one unit. And what it will cost the builder: the labour and the material.
The builder quotes, the client compares, and they agree.
Then the contract: the price, the dates, and the rules for how money moves for the next nine months.

scenes.title: What the architect drew
beats: These are Green Villa's drawings: eight sheets from the architect and the consultants. This one is A-101, the ground floor plan.
Every room, every wall, every door and window, drawn to scale. The BOQ's quantities are measured off sheets like this one.
Bedroom one is four point two metres by three point six. Its label says a hundred and sixty-three square feet, and that is right.
Bedroom two is three point six by three point six. Its label also says a hundred and sixty-three. Keep that in mind: we will come back to it.

scenes.title: One line, four numbers
beats: Take one line of Green Villa's BOQ: plastering the inside walls. One thousand four hundred and fifty square metres.
The client pays four hundred and twenty rupees for each square metre.
It costs the builder three hundred and thirty: two hundred and ten for labour, a hundred and twenty for cement and sand.
So every square metre plastered leaves ninety rupees. On the whole line, about one lakh thirty thousand. Green Villa has thirty-four lines like this one, in nine sections.

scenes.title: The whole estimate, in Excel
beats: And here is the whole estimate, as Ramesh priced it in Excel: the item number, the work, the unit, the quantity, the client's rate, and his own labour and material cost.
There is the plastering line: one thousand four hundred and fifty square metres, at four hundred and twenty.
Two things are hiding in this sheet. The staircase: the client's rate is seven thousand nine hundred, but labour and material add up to eight thousand two hundred.
And the tiling: the client's rate is there, but the cost columns are empty. Nobody has the tiler's price yet.

scenes.title: The BOQ is the yardstick for everything after
beats: Here is why the BOQ matters so much. It is not a document you file away. Everything after day one is measured against it.
Every piece of work the site reports lands on a BOQ line, so you know how far each line has got.
The material each line needs comes from it. So does the check on whether the labour was worth the work it did.
A subcontractor is measured and paid on its lines. And every month, the client is billed for the quantity done on each line, at its rate.
And at any moment, comparing what each line earned with what it really cost tells you if the job is making money.
Get the BOQ wrong, and every one of these is wrong too.

scenes.title: What the contract adds
beats: The contract adds the rules for money and time. Eighty-two lakh rupees for the work, with GST at eighteen percent on top.
A mobilisation advance: ten percent, about eight lakh twenty thousand, paid at the start so the builder can set up the site. It is taken back, ten percent from every bill, until it is all recovered.
Retention: five percent of every bill is held back by the client, and released only when the defects period ends, twelve months after handover.
Bills every month, on the work measured, at the BOQ rates, paid within fifteen days.
And handover on the thirty-first of July. Every week late costs twenty-five thousand rupees.

scenes.eyebrow: What the terms do to cash
scenes.title: ₹10 lakh of work: what reaches the bank
beats: See what those terms do to cash. Say the site does ten lakh rupees of work in a month, at the BOQ rates.
One lakh is taken back against the advance the builder already received.
Fifty thousand is held as retention, for well over a year.
So eight and a half lakh is what the company gets to spend this month. GST of one lakh eighty thousand comes in on top, and goes straight on to the government.
A builder who plans on the full ten lakh will run short, every single month.

scenes.note: GST ₹1,80,000 is added on top and passed to the government. Green Villa's client is a person, so no TDS.

scenes.title: Who does what, before the first brick
beats: Who does what, before the first brick?
The architect and the structural consultant make the drawings.
Ramesh Nair, the owner of Green Villa Builders, measures the BOQ, sets the rates, quotes, and signs the contract.
Doctor Krishnan, the client, pays the advance, and later, each month's bill.
And two people who will live by this paper for nine months: Anil, the project manager, who counts the work against the BOQ; and Meera in accounts, who bills the client and recovers the advance.

scenes.title: Three things in, before anything else
beats: Now, in Mesiri. A new project opens on Project start: everything the office must put in before the site's records mean anything.
The dates from the contract: work starts on the second of November, handover on the thirty-first of July.
The client and the contract: the value, the advance, the retention, the defects period. Typed once, from the contract summary.
And the BOQ. Each step ticks itself the moment it is saved. Nobody marks anything done by hand.

scenes.title: The estimate goes in as it is
beats: The BOQ is not typed again. The estimate Ramesh priced in Excel goes in as it is.
Mesiri reads the columns: the item number, the work, the unit, the quantity, the client's rate, the labour and the material cost.
It shows what it read before anything is saved: nine sections, thirty-four lines, and the totals.
And it says what is not finished: three lines have no cost yet. The tiling and the granite are waiting for the tiler's price.

scenes.title: Green Villa at a glance
beats: This is the BOQ page. Across the top, Green Villa at a glance.
What the client pays: eighty-two lakh. What it should cost: sixty-one lakh, seventy-five percent of the contract.
The margin, on the lines that have a cost: thirteen lakh, about eighteen percent. Marked not final, because three lines have no cost yet.
Thirty-one of thirty-four lines are priced. Until the tiler's price is in, nobody should quote a profit figure for this job.

scenes.eyebrow: In Mesiri · A line in red
scenes.title: A loss decided at the tender
beats: Look down the margin column. One line is red.
The staircase waist slab: seven thousand nine hundred rupees a cubic metre from the client, eight thousand two hundred to build.
Every cubic metre loses three hundred rupees. Nine cubic metres: two thousand seven hundred.
Small, but it was decided the day the price was written. Mesiri shows it before the first bag of cement is used, not at the end.

scenes.eyebrow: In Mesiri · The yardstick at work
scenes.title: The site's work, on its lines
beats: In the sample company you will play, you meet Green Villa seven months in, and the office has only now put the BOQ in. That happens on real jobs too. For two weeks Ravi, the site engineer, has sent each day's work on WhatsApp: twenty-four pieces of work, waiting for a BOQ.
Mesiri matched twenty-one of them to their lines by name and unit. Three just said plastering, and the BOQ has three plastering lines, so a person chose.
Now each line shows how far it has got. The annex: site clearance twenty-seven percent, excavation twenty-three, the footings twenty-six.
The months before Mesiri are on paper, so this counts from here. From now on, every message from site moves these bars by itself.

scenes.title: Five ways a job is lost on paper
beats: Five ways a job is lost before the first brick.
A line priced below its cost, like the staircase. And lines with no cost at all, which make the margin look bigger than it is.
Work with no line. Green Villa's estimate has no line for putty and primer. The site will do it, and it can never be billed.
A quantity taken from a wrong label. Remember bedroom two: drawn at about a hundred and forty square feet, labelled a hundred and sixty-three. Measure from the label, and the BOQ is wrong.
And contract terms nobody reads: the advance coming back out of every bill, the retention, and twenty-five thousand rupees for every week late.

footer.text: Each one is fixed for free on paper, and paid for on site.

scenes.title: Three questions
beats: Three questions. Pause, and answer them before you go on.
One: why is the BOQ called the yardstick? Because everything after it, the site's work, material, labour, the bills and the profit, is measured against its lines.

Two: of ten lakh rupees of work in a month, how much does Green Villa Builders get to spend? Eight and a half lakh: one lakh goes back against the advance, fifty thousand is retention, and the GST passes to the government.
Three: name one thing on paper that loses money on site. A line priced below cost, a line with no cost, work with no line, a quantity copied wrong, or terms nobody read.
